record.tranche_reason: Compares two differently sized speech-language models and reports evaluation results on speech continuation, extending scale-related performance testing to a speech-generation setting.
record.gate_note: The report compares TTS-1 and TTS-1-Max on prompt-continuation speaker similarity and explicitly describes the larger model's gains. Its pretraining-loss and benchmark figures are not reported as power-law fits, held-out loss scaling, or extrapolation tests. Other codec, RL, and inference results do not bear on the claim versions.
record.test_reason: This is a product technical report for two TTS models (1B and 8B LLaMA backbones). It scales model size as a design choice and reports only its own models' performance. It fits no power law, does no extrapolation or allocation sweep, and has no multi-size series. A two-point size comparison cannot show whether downstream performance improves predictably (V6), or whether a power-law form holds in speech (V5). The finding is relied on, not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but it omits the main conclusion. The authors mainly conclude that a three-stage pipeline (pre-training, SFT, GRPO RL alignment) plus a 48 kHz codec yields state-of-the-art TTS. A secondary point is that the larger TTS-1-Max outperforms TTS-1 across evaluations. They also say pre-trained checkpoint performance correlates with the two models' training-loss difference.
record.recipe_differences: This is a speech-generation report, not a reproduction of the original scaling-law method. It compares two model sizes and does not fit scaling laws or test extrapolation.
record.method_sensitivity: The report notes that cross-language results are not directly comparable because each language subset contains different utterances.

fits_no_version.finding: The 8B-backbone TTS-1-Max has lower pretraining loss and outperforms the 1B TTS-1. It does better on prompt-continuation SIM (Fig. 4) and on multilingual WER and SIM (Fig. 8). English WER is 5.1% vs 6.3% overall (Table 8), and the larger model wins 55.3% of head-to-head human votes (Table 9).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In speech-language TTS models, a larger LLM backbone with lower pretraining loss gives better downstream speech quality. This is a two-point comparison, not a scaling law.

record.problems: Only two model sizes are compared for the relevant evaluation; the report gives no numerical values for the Figure 4 comparison in the text and no uncertainty estimates. The test set uses distinct utterances across language subsets.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows were included: the report does not state results for the other claim versions.

untested.parts: No held-out loss versus parameters, tokens or compute fit. Figure 3 shows loss curves for only two models.
No fit on small runs and no prediction of larger runs.
No shape ablation at a fixed parameter count.
No power-law form is tested for speech-token pretraining, fine-tuning or RL.
There is no scale series or loss-to-task fit. Only two model sizes are compared on SIM and WER.
No exponents or fitting choices are examined.

record.verdict_notes: The study cites Hoffmann et al. and speaks of 'scaling train-time compute'. It is not a scaling-law study, so no verdicts are given. The size comparison is confounded only by small hyperparameter differences, but with two points it cannot bear on the predictability versions.

versions.untested_parts: No test of held-out pretraining loss as a power law in parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fit or prediction of much larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token split.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architectures at fixed parameter count.
The study concerns speech generation but does not test whether a power-law form holds in this setting or other modalities and training regimes.
Tests only a comparison of two model sizes on prompt-continuation similarity; it does not fit a predictive relationship or test downstream tasks generally.
No comparison of fitting choices, exponents, or curve departures from a power law.

rows.subject: TTS-1-Max
rows.size_stated: 8.8B parameters with inference components; SpeechLM backbone LLaMA-3.1-8B
rows.operation_detail: Compared speech-generation performance across two SpeechLM model sizes.

conditions.value: prompt continuation; multilingual test set of approximately 5,000 utterances, average duration 10 seconds

rows.value: The report states that prompt-continuation similarity improvements are more pronounced for TTS-1-Max than for TTS-1; figure values are not stated in the text.
rows.note: The report says overall performance correlates with the difference in training loss between the models. It also cautions that cross-language results are not directly comparable because language subsets contain distinct utterances.
rows.check: This two-size comparison (TTS-1 vs TTS-1-Max) on prompt-continuation SIM cannot show a predictable or power-law relation, so it bears on no version. Figure 4 values are not readable from the text. 'Partial' was also unsupported: the text says the larger model's gains are more pronounced, which is a direction, not a weaker effect.

source_check.locator_found: Section 2; Section 3.3, evaluation results and Figure 4 caption.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

rows.locator_found: Section 2; Section 3.3, evaluation results and Figure 4 caption.

relation.reason: The two-size performance comparison and qualitative association with training loss do not establish the predictability required by V6 or test the other claim versions.

tranche.reason: Uses increased model size and training compute in developing its TTS systems; reports their performance without fitting or testing a scaling law or predictive relationship.

source_check.notes: Section 3.3 corroborates the qualitative SIM improvement and evaluation conditions; Figure 4 supplies no readable numerical SIM values in the extracted text. Cross-language results are not directly comparable because language subsets contain different utterances.
